--- title: "Module 6 · Capstone: your own analysis" subtitle: "Plan, run and document a reproducible APC analysis of your data" ---

MODULE 6 OF 6 · ABOUT 2 HOURS · PROJECT

By the end of this module you will have

  • written a one-paragraph brief that links your question to the right method;
  • prepared your data as a rates object and checked it;
  • run a short analysis script from data to estimable functions;
  • organized the project so that someone else can rerun it.
  • 6.1 Plan your question
  • 6.2 Prepare your data
  • 6.3 Analyse
  • 6.4 Make it reproducible
  • Self-assessment
Reading15 min
## Plan your question {#plan-your-question} Write a brief of one paragraph: *which population, which outcome, which ages and years, and what you want to learn.* Then pick the module that fits: | Your question | Method | Module | |---|---|---| | Are rates rising or falling, and at which ages? | New APC model: net drift, local drifts | [2](m2-new-apc-model.qmd) | | Is the pattern the same in women and men, or in two countries? | CAPRICORN | [3](m3-capricorn.qmd) | | Are younger generations at higher risk than their parents' generation? | Generation means and proxy-parent contrasts | [4](m4-generations-shares.qmd) | | What share of deaths is due to this cause, by cohort? | `fcp_share()` | [4](m4-generations-shares.qmd) | ::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"} Write your brief now. Example: "Cervical cancer incidence in women aged 20 to 84 in registry X, 1998 to 2017. Are rates changing, and does the pattern differ between cohorts born before and after 1960?" :::
Hands-on lab30 min
## Prepare your data {#prepare-your-data} Follow Module 1. In short: 1. **Get counts and person-years** by age and year from your registry or from [SEER*Stat](https://seer.cancer.gov/seerstat/) or [CI5 Plus](https://ci5.iarc.fr/). The [Resources](../resources.qmd) page links slides that show how. 2. **Build a rates object**: `csv2rates()` for a file in the NCI web tool format, or `rates_make()` for a table with `age`, `year`, `cases` and `py`. 3. **Make the cells square** with `rates_chunk()` (for example 5-year ages by 5-year periods). 4. **Check** `rates_uni(R)`. How many cases are there? Are many cells empty? If so, use wider cells before using `rates_fill()`. Keep your raw data files exactly as you received them. Do all cleaning in scripts.
Hands-on lab45 min
## Analyse {#analyse} This script is the shortest useful analysis. It runs here on example 5 (synthetic breast cancer); replace the first line with your own data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} R <- matisse_example(5) # your data: csv2rates("my_rates.csv") R5 <- rates_fill(rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5)) M <- apc_fit(R5) # New APC model E <- apc_efs(M) # LAC, CAC, FTT, FCP and local drifts round(M$net_drift, 2) # percent per year ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0.77 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} f <- apc_fcp(M, age = 60) # cohort pattern at a chosen age fcp_generations(f)$table[, .(generation, n, mean = round(mean, 1))] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|generation | n| mean| |:----------------------------|--:|-----:| |Greatest | 3| 205.1| |Silent | 4| 232.6| |Boomers | 3| 268.0| |GenX | 4| 302.8| |Millennials | NA| NA| |Proxy parents of Boomers | 5| 220.0| |Proxy parents of GenX | 5| 257.4| |Proxy parents of Millennials | 5| 289.9|
::: ::: From here, add what your brief needs: - **Compare groups:** build a named list of rates objects and call `capricorn()` (Module 3). - **Contrast generations:** `fcp_contrast(f)` and `ld_onset(M)` (Module 4). - **Save tables**, not only figures: `fwrite(E, "output/apc/estimable_functions.csv")`.
Reading20 min
## Make it reproducible {#make-it-reproducible} The Europe case study follows a set of habits that make their results easy to check and to reuse. Adopt the same habits in your project: - **One README** with the purpose, the data sources and the **run order**. - **Numbered scripts** that each do one step and write to their own folder. - **Never edit raw data.** Read it, and write derived data elsewhere. - **A data dictionary in every output folder**: a small CSV that lists each file and variable with a description, unit and provenance. - **Record your software:** a script that writes the R and package versions to a text file. - **Rerun without surprises:** relative paths, and `set.seed()` wherever random numbers are used. - **Read numbers from outputs**, not from memory, when you write a report. ``` my-apc-project/ |-- README.md purpose, data sources, run order |-- code/ | |-- 00_session.R writes output/session_info.txt | |-- 01_rates.R raw files -> data/derived/rates.rds | |-- 02_apc.R apc_fit, apc_efs -> output/apc/ | `-- 03_figures.R output/apc/*.csv -> figures |-- data/ | |-- raw/ as received, never edited | `-- derived/ `-- output/ `-- apc/ |-- estimable_functions.csv `-- dictionary.csv ``` A dictionary can be as simple as this: | file | variable | description | unit | |---|---|---|---| | estimable_functions.csv | ef | estimable function: lac, cac, ftt, fcp or ld | | | estimable_functions.csv | x | age, period or cohort midpoint | years | | estimable_functions.csv | value | estimate | rate per 100,000, or % per year for ld | | estimable_functions.csv | lo, hi | 95% confidence limits | as `value` |
Self-assessment10 min
## Self-assessment {#self-assessment} Check your project against this list: - [ ] My brief names the population, outcome, ages, years and question. - [ ] The rates object has square cells, and I know how many zero cells I filled. - [ ] I report the net drift with its interval and name the reference age I used for any cohort pattern. - [ ] If I compared groups, I looked at the global tests **and** AICc, and I used `overdispersion = TRUE` for real counts. - [ ] Anyone can rerun my scripts from the README, in order, and get the same tables. ::: {.quiz data-answer="3"} **Which file should every output folder of your project contain?** 1. The raw data. 2. A copy of the R installer. 3. A data dictionary describing each file and variable. ::: explain A dictionary makes outputs findable and reusable: it records what each variable means, its unit, and which script wrote it. Raw data stay in their own folder and are never edited. ::: ::: Questions about your project? Write to matisse.apc@gmail.com. When you are ready, revisit the [Europe case study](../cases/eu-generations.qmd) to see a project organized in this way.
